title: Employee leave requests
scenario: Approving a leave updates the balance in memory but not in the database, depending on which method ran.
stack: Spring Boot 4.1.1 · Java 25 · Spring Data JPA (Hibernate 7) · @Transactional · @Version · @DataJpaTest · PostgreSQL 17 · Flyway · Testcontainers
simulation: Employees, balances and requests are demo data, not Teamdesk's. Approving creates a record and changes a number; no payroll, calendar or email is involved. Weekends are free; public holidays are not modelled (a demo rule).

Level 1, about 5 minutes. Plain language: no code.

The problem in real life

  1. The balance that did not move

    Teamdesk's HR found employees with approved leave and an untouched balance. The manager's screen had shown the right number at approval: 12 days, 3 approved, 9 left.

  2. It depended on the method

    Approvals from the mobile app were fine; approvals from the web inbox were not. Both called the same lines of code, but only one of them ran inside a transaction.

  3. The fix

    One transactional service method that loads the request and the employee, changes both, and lets Hibernate write both at commit.

A change to an object is saved only while Hibernate is watching it, and Hibernate watches only inside a transaction.

What are we building?

An employee asks for leave (POST /leave-requests); a manager approves it (POST /leave-requests/{id}/approval), which marks the request approved and takes the days off the balance; anyone can read the balance (GET /employees/{id}/leave-balance). The request and the balance always change together.

An everyday analogy

A clerk with a desk. While the cards are on the desk, any correction goes into the file when the clerk closes for the day. A photocopy taken home can be corrected all evening; the file never hears of it. The old code corrected the photocopy of the employee's card, and refiled only the leave form.

How it works in 4 steps

  1. The approval starts a transaction, with a fresh persistence context.
  2. It loads the request and its employee: both are now managed.
  3. It checks and changes them in memory: status APPROVED, balance minus the days.
  4. At commit, Hibernate finds both changes and writes both rows, or neither.
Check yourself: the fixed approve never calls save(). How do the changes reach the database?

Both entities were loaded inside the transaction, so they are managed. At commit, Hibernate compares them with what it loaded (dirty checking) and writes an UPDATE for each one that changed.

What this station is not

  • No login. Anyone may approve; a real desk checks the manager.
  • No holidays or half days. Monday to Friday count; nothing else is modelled.
  • No overlap check. Two requests for the same days are both accepted.

Level 2. What a teammate hands you before you build.

Business problem

Teamdesk (a fictional HR SaaS) approves leave and keeps each employee's balance. Approvals saved the request but sometimes not the balance, depending on which code path ran.

Acceptance criteria

  1. Given Asha asks for Friday 6 to Tuesday 10 November 2026, then 201, 3 working days, PENDING, and her balance is still 12.
  2. Given the manager approves it, then 200, and both the response and GET show 9.
  3. Given it is approved again, then 409 and the balance stays 9.
  4. Given Rohan has 2 days and asks for 3, then approval is 422 and nothing changes.
  5. Given 8 managers approve the same request at the same moment, then one 200, seven 409, and 3 days are taken once.
  6. Given a malformed body, 400; impossible dates or an unknown employee, 422; an unknown request or employee in the path, 404.

Requirements

  • Approval changes the request and the balance in one transaction.
  • A balance never goes below zero, and a request is approved at most once, also in the database.
  • Days are counted on the server: Monday to Friday, at most 42 calendar days per request (demo rules).
  • Two approvals at once never lose a deduction.

Learning objectives

  • Explain the persistence context: managed and detached entities, dirty checking.
  • Put @Transactional on the service method that owns a business change.
  • Know what save() does on a managed entity (nothing) and on a detached one (merge, returning a copy).
  • Write a @DataJpaTest, and know what its automatic transaction can hide.

Every edge case points at the test that proves it.

Edge cases

CaseWhat happensProved by

Approve, then read the balanceBoth say 9approvalTakesTheDaysAndTheBalanceShowsIt
Approve twice409, deducted onceaDecidedRequestCannotBeApprovedAgain

6 different requests approved at onceEach 200 took its days; the rest are 409 or 422approvingDifferentRequestsAtOnceNeverLosesADeduction

The trap

Plausible but wrong

Changing a managed entity outside a transaction and expecting it to be saved.

The old desk, kept in the tests, has no @Transactional. Each repository call runs in its own short transaction, so the request and employee it loads are detached when the call returns. It sets the status and the balance, then calls requests.save(request): a merge, which copies the request's own columns and nothing from the employee, because the association is not cascaded. The manager sees 9; the database keeps 12.

The second test runs the very same lines inside a transaction: both rows are saved, with no extra code. That is the "depends on which method ran" in the bug report.

While building, each part was undone once. Removing @Transactional from approve turned 5 tests red; removing @Version from Employee 1 (the parallel test with different requests); removing the PENDING check 2; removing the balance check 1. Removing @Version from LeaveRequest turned none red: every approval also changes the employee, whose version already catches the race. It is kept because rejecting (challenge 1) changes only the request.

package com.teamdesk.leave;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionTemplate;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

/**
 * The first test written for this station: the old approval, run the way production ran it. The same lines save
 * everything or half of it, depending only on whether a transaction was open around them.
 */
class DetachedEntityTrapTest extends ApiTest {

    @Autowired
    TransactionTemplate transaction;

    @Test
    void withoutATransactionTheManagerSeesNineButTheDatabaseKeepsTwelve() throws Exception {
        long id = newRequest(1, "2026-11-06", "2026-11-10");
        int shown = new OldLeaveDesk(requests).approve(id);
        assertThat(shown).isEqualTo(9);
        assertThat(statusInTheDatabase(id)).isEqualTo("APPROVED");   // the request was saved...
        assertThat(balanceInTheDatabase(1)).isEqualTo(12);           // ...the balance was not: 3 days of leave for free
    }

    @Test
    void theSameLinesInsideATransactionSaveBoth() throws Exception {
        long id = newRequest(1, "2026-11-06", "2026-11-10");
        transaction.executeWithoutResult(status -> new OldLeaveDesk(requests).approve(id));
        assertThat(statusInTheDatabase(id)).isEqualTo("APPROVED");
        assertThat(balanceInTheDatabase(1)).isEqualTo(9);   // dirty checking wrote the employee too
    }

    @Test
    void theFixedDeskSavesBothWithoutCallingSave() throws Exception {
        long id = newRequest(1, "2026-11-06", "2026-11-10");
        approve(id);
        assertThat(statusInTheDatabase(id)).isEqualTo("APPROVED");
        assertThat(balanceInTheDatabase(1)).isEqualTo(9);
    }
}
package com.teamdesk.leave;

/**
 * The approval as it shipped, kept to reproduce the bug. No @Transactional: each repository call runs in its own
 * short transaction, so the entities it returns are detached the moment it returns.
 */
class OldLeaveDesk {

    private final LeaveRequestRepository requests;

    OldLeaveDesk(LeaveRequestRepository requests) {
        this.requests = requests;
    }

    /** Returns the balance it showed the manager. */
    int approve(long id) {
        LeaveRequest request = requests.findWithEmployeeById(id).orElseThrow();
        request.approve();       // status APPROVED, and the employee's balance goes down: in memory
        requests.save(request);  // merge copies the request's columns; the employee is not cascaded, so its change is dropped
        return request.getEmployee().getBalanceDays();
    }
}

import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank;

import org.springframework.dao.OptimisticLockingFailureException;

import org.springframework.http.ProblemDetail;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ExceptionHandler;

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ResponseStatus;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

import java.time.LocalDate;

@RestController
class LeaveController {

    record NewRequest(@NotNull Long employeeId, @NotNull LocalDate startDate, @NotNull LocalDate endDate,
                      @NotBlank @Size(max = 200) String reason) {
    }

    private final LeaveDesk desk;

    LeaveController(LeaveDesk desk) {
        this.desk = desk;
    }

    @PostMapping("/leave-requests")
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
    LeaveDesk.RequestView request(@Valid @RequestBody NewRequest body) {
        return desk.request(body.employeeId(), body.startDate(), body.endDate(), body.reason().strip());
    }

    /** Demo: no login, so anyone may approve. A real desk checks that the caller is the employee's manager. */
    @PostMapping("/leave-requests/{id}/approval")
    LeaveDesk.ApprovalView approve(@PathVariable long id) {
        return desk.approve(id);
    }

    @GetMapping("/employees/{id}/leave-balance")
    LeaveDesk.BalanceView balance(@PathVariable long id) {
        return desk.balance(id);
    }

    /** A @Version check failed at commit: another approval changed the request or the balance first. */
    @ExceptionHandler(OptimisticLockingFailureException.class)
    ProblemDetail changedMeanwhile() {
        ProblemDetail p = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT,
                "Another approval changed this request or this balance at the same moment. Reload and try again.");
        p.setTitle("Changed meanwhile");
        return p;
    }

src/main/java/com/teamdesk/leave/LeaveDesk.java

Does
Counts working days, creates requests, approves them, reads balances.
Why
approve is one transaction and calls no save().
Without it
Half-saved approvals.
  • The checks (PENDING, enough days) run on the loaded entities, then request.approve() changes both.
  • The response is built inside the transaction, from the same objects that are about to be written.
  • Errors are ErrorResponseException with a ProblemDetail; the transaction rolls back on them.
package com.teamdesk.leave;

import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.ProblemDetail;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;
import org.springframework.web.ErrorResponseException;

import java.time.DayOfWeek;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit;

@Service
class LeaveDesk {

    /** Demo rule: a request spans at most 6 weeks (so at most 30 working days). Weekends are free; holidays are not modelled. */
    static final int MAX_SPAN_DAYS = 42;

    record RequestView(long id, long employeeId, LocalDate startDate, LocalDate endDate, int days, String reason, String status) {
        static RequestView of(LeaveRequest r) {
            return new RequestView(r.getId(), r.getEmployee().getId(), r.getStartDate(), r.getEndDate(), r.getDays(), r.getReason(), r.getStatus().name());
        }
    }

    record ApprovalView(long requestId, String status, int days, long employeeId, int balanceDays) {
    }

    record BalanceView(long employeeId, String name, int balanceDays) {
    }

    private final EmployeeRepository employees;
    private final LeaveRequestRepository requests;

    LeaveDesk(EmployeeRepository employees, LeaveRequestRepository requests) {
        this.employees = employees;
        this.requests = requests;
    }

    @Transactional
    RequestView request(long employeeId, LocalDate start, LocalDate end, String reason) {
        if (end.isBefore(start)) {
            throw problem(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT, "Invalid dates", "endDate is before startDate.");
        }
        if (ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(start, end) >= MAX_SPAN_DAYS) {
            throw problem(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT, "Invalid dates", "A request covers at most " + MAX_SPAN_DAYS + " calendar days.");
        }
        int days = workingDays(start, end);
        if (days == 0) {
            throw problem(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT, "No working days", "Every date from " + start + " to " + end + " is a weekend.");
        }
        Employee employee = employees.findById(employeeId)
                .orElseThrow(() -> problem(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT, "Unknown employee", "No employee " + employeeId + "."));
        return RequestView.of(requests.save(new LeaveRequest(employee, start, end, days, reason)));
    }

    /**
     * One transaction: the request and the employee are loaded into one persistence context, changed in memory, and
     * written together when the method returns. There is no save() call, and none is needed.
     */
    @Transactional
    ApprovalView approve(long id) {
        LeaveRequest request = requests.findWithEmployeeById(id)
                .orElseThrow(() -> problem(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Leave request not found", "No leave request " + id + "."));
        if (request.getStatus() != LeaveRequest.Status.PENDING) {
            throw problem(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "Already decided", "Leave request " + id + " is already " + request.getStatus() + ".");
        }
        Employee employee = request.getEmployee();
        if (employee.getBalanceDays() < request.getDays()) {
            throw problem(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT, "Not enough leave",
                    employee.getName() + " has " + employee.getBalanceDays() + " days left; this request needs " + request.getDays() + ".");
        }
        request.approve();
        return new ApprovalView(id, request.getStatus().name(), request.getDays(), employee.getId(), employee.getBalanceDays());
    }

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    BalanceView balance(long employeeId) {
        return employees.findById(employeeId).map(e -> new BalanceView(e.getId(), e.getName(), e.getBalanceDays()))
                .orElseThrow(() -> problem(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Employee not found", "No employee " + employeeId + "."));
    }

    static int workingDays(LocalDate start, LocalDate end) {
        return (int) start.datesUntil(end.plusDays(1))
                .filter(d -> d.getDayOfWeek() != DayOfWeek.SATURDAY && d.getDayOfWeek() != DayOfWeek.SUNDAY).count();
    }

    static ErrorResponseException problem(HttpStatus status, String title, String detail) {
        ProblemDetail p = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(status, detail);
        p.setTitle(title);
        return new ErrorResponseException(status, p, null);
    }
}

Why

Two decisions on the same request at once.
package com.teamdesk.leave;

import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.EnumType;
import jakarta.persistence.Enumerated;
import jakarta.persistence.FetchType;
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue;
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import jakarta.persistence.JoinColumn;
import jakarta.persistence.ManyToOne;
import jakarta.persistence.Table;
import jakarta.persistence.Version;

import java.time.LocalDate;

@Entity
@Table(name = "leave_requests")
public class LeaveRequest {

    public enum Status { PENDING, APPROVED, REJECTED }

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "employee_id")
    private Employee employee;
    private LocalDate startDate;
    private LocalDate endDate;
    private int days;
    private String reason;
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private Status status = Status.PENDING;
    @Version
    private long version;

    protected LeaveRequest() {
    }

    LeaveRequest(Employee employee, LocalDate startDate, LocalDate endDate, int days, String reason) {
        this.employee = employee;
        this.startDate = startDate;
        this.endDate = endDate;
        this.days = days;
        this.reason = reason;
    }

    /** Changes two objects: this request and the employee's balance. Only a managed pair is saved by itself. */
    void approve() {
        status = Status.APPROVED;
        employee.deduct(days);
    }

    public Long getId() {
        return id;
    }

    public Employee getEmployee() {
        return employee;
    }

    public LocalDate getStartDate() {
        return startDate;
    }

    public LocalDate getEndDate() {
        return endDate;
    }

    public int getDays() {
        return days;
    }

    public String getReason() {
        return reason;
    }

    public Status getStatus() {
        return status;
    }
}

package com.teamdesk.leave;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionTemplate;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

/** The tables' rules with Java bypassed, a rollback across both rows, and approvals racing each other. */
class LeaveDatabaseTest extends ApiTest {

    @Autowired
    TransactionTemplate transaction;

    void insert(long employee, String start, String end, int days, String status) {
        jdbc.sql("INSERT INTO leave_requests (employee_id, start_date, end_date, days, reason, status) VALUES (?, ?::date, ?::date, ?, 'Test', ?)")
                .params(employee, start, end, days, status).update();
    }

    @Test
    void namedConstraintsHoldWithoutJava() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> jdbc.sql("UPDATE employees SET balance_days = -1 WHERE id = 1").update()).hasMessageContaining("employees_balance_not_negative");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> insert(99, "2026-11-06", "2026-11-10", 3, "PENDING")).hasMessageContaining("leave_requests_employee_fk");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> insert(1, "2026-11-10", "2026-11-06", 3, "PENDING")).hasMessageContaining("leave_requests_dates_ordered");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> insert(1, "2026-11-06", "2026-11-10", 0, "PENDING")).hasMessageContaining("leave_requests_days_range");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> insert(1, "2026-11-06", "2026-11-10", 6, "PENDING")).hasMessageContaining("leave_requests_days_fit_dates");
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> insert(1, "2026-11-06", "2026-11-10", 3, "MAYBE")).hasMessageContaining("leave_requests_status_known");
    }

    @Test
    void whenTheBalanceWriteFailsTheApprovalRollsBackToo() throws Exception {
        long id = newRequest(2, "2026-11-06", "2026-11-10");   // 3 days; Rohan has 2
        // Skip the Java balance check: the database refuses -1, and the request's change goes with it.
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> transaction.executeWithoutResult(status -> requests.findWithEmployeeById(id).orElseThrow().approve()))
                .hasMessageContaining("employees_balance_not_negative");
        assertThat(statusInTheDatabase(id)).isEqualTo("PENDING");
        assertThat(balanceInTheDatabase(2)).isEqualTo(2);
    }

    @Test
    void eightManagersApprovingTheSameRequestDeductOnce() throws Exception {
        long id = newRequest(1, "2026-11-06", "2026-11-10");
        List<Integer> statuses = together(8, () -> approve(id).andReturn().getResponse().getStatus());
        assertThat(statuses).filteredOn(s -> s == 200).hasSize(1);
        assertThat(statuses).filteredOn(s -> s == 409).hasSize(7);
        assertThat(balanceInTheDatabase(1)).isEqualTo(9);
    }

    @Test
    void approvingDifferentRequestsAtOnceNeverLosesADeduction() throws Exception {
        AtomicInteger next = new AtomicInteger();
        long[] ids = new long[6];
        for (int i = 0; i < ids.length; i++) {   // six Mon-Wed requests (3 days each) from Asha, who has 12: four fit
            LocalDate monday = LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2).plusWeeks(i);
            ids[i] = newRequest(1, monday.toString(), monday.plusDays(2).toString());
        }
        List<Integer> statuses = together(ids.length, () -> approve(ids[next.getAndIncrement()]).andReturn().getResponse().getStatus());
        assertThat(statuses).isSubsetOf(200, 409, 422);   // a 409 means "reload and retry", never a lost deduction
        long approved = jdbc.sql("SELECT count(*) FROM leave_requests WHERE status = 'APPROVED'").query(Long.class).single();
        assertThat(approved).isEqualTo(statuses.stream().filter(s -> s == 200).count()).isPositive();
        assertThat(balanceInTheDatabase(1)).isEqualTo(12 - 3 * (int) approved);   // every approval's deduction is there
    }
}

package com.teamdesk.leave;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.data.jpa.test.autoconfigure.DataJpaTest;
import org.springframework.boot.jdbc.test.autoconfigure.AutoConfigureTestDatabase;
import org.springframework.boot.jpa.test.autoconfigure.TestEntityManager;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Import;

import java.time.LocalDate;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

/**
 * A @DataJpaTest: only JPA, on the real PostgreSQL, and every test runs inside one transaction that is rolled back at
 * the end. That transaction keeps every entity managed, which is exactly what the old approval lacked in production.
 */
@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)   // keep PostgreSQL, not an in-memory database
@Import(PostgresTestConfig.class)
class LeaveJpaTest {

    @Autowired
    TestEntityManager entities;
    @Autowired
    EmployeeRepository employees;
    @Autowired
    LeaveRequestRepository requests;

    int balanceInTheDatabase(long id) {
        entities.flush();   // send pending changes now; the test's rollback still undoes them afterwards
        return ((Number) entities.getEntityManager().createNativeQuery("SELECT balance_days FROM employees WHERE id = ?1")
                .setParameter(1, id).getSingleResult()).intValue();
    }

    @Test
    void aManagedEntityIsWrittenWithoutSave() {
        Employee asha = employees.findById(1L).orElseThrow();
        asha.deduct(3);   // no save(): dirty checking finds the change at flush
        assertThat(balanceInTheDatabase(1)).isEqualTo(9);
    }

    @Test
    void saveOnAManagedEntityReturnsTheSameObject() {
        Employee asha = employees.findById(1L).orElseThrow();
        assertThat(employees.save(asha)).isSameAs(asha);   // JPA has no update(): save here does nothing at all
    }

    @Test
    void saveOnADetachedEntityReturnsACopyAndOnlyTheCopyIsTracked() {
        Employee asha = employees.findById(1L).orElseThrow();
        entities.detach(asha);
        asha.deduct(3);
        Employee managed = employees.save(asha);   // merge: loads the row and copies asha's fields onto a managed copy
        assertThat(managed).isNotSameAs(asha);
        asha.deduct(5);   // the copy you passed in is still detached: this change goes nowhere
        assertThat(balanceInTheDatabase(1)).isEqualTo(9);
        managed.deduct(1);
        assertThat(balanceInTheDatabase(1)).isEqualTo(8);
    }

    @Test
    void theOldApprovalPassesHereWhichIsHowTheBugShipped() {
        LeaveRequest request = requests.save(new LeaveRequest(employees.findById(1L).orElseThrow(),
                LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 6), LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 10), 3, "Sister's wedding in Jaipur"));
        new OldLeaveDesk(requests).approve(request.getId());
        // Green: the test's own transaction kept the employee managed. DetachedEntityTrapTest runs the same code
        // without one, as production did, and the balance stays at 12.
        assertThat(balanceInTheDatabase(1)).isEqualTo(9);
    }
}

    /** Runs n copies of the task on virtual threads, all released together by one latch. */
    static <T> List<T> together(int n, Callable<T> task) throws Exception {
        CountDownLatch start = new CountDownLatch(1);
        List<Future<T>> futures = new ArrayList<>();
        try (ExecutorService threads = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
                futures.add(threads.submit(() -> {
                    start.await();
                    return task.call();
                }));
            }
            start.countDown();
        }
        List<T> results = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Future<T> f : futures) {

        static RequestView of(LeaveRequest r) {

        }
    }

    record ApprovalView(long requestId, String status, int days, long employeeId, int balanceDays) {
    }

    record BalanceView(long employeeId, String name, int balanceDays) {
    }

    private final EmployeeRepository employees;
    private final LeaveRequestRepository requests;

    LeaveDesk(EmployeeRepository employees, LeaveRequestRepository requests) {
        this.employees = employees;
        this.requests = requests;
    }

    @Transactional
    RequestView request(long employeeId, LocalDate start, LocalDate end, String reason) {
        if (end.isBefore(start)) {
            throw problem(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT, "Invalid dates", "endDate is before startDate.");
        }
        if (ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(start, end) >= MAX_SPAN_DAYS) {
            throw problem(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT, "Invalid dates", "A request covers at most " + MAX_SPAN_DAYS + " calendar days.");
        }
        int days = workingDays(start, end);
        if (days == 0) {
            throw problem(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT, "No working days", "Every date from " + start + " to " + end + " is a weekend.");
        }
        Employee employee = employees.findById(employeeId)
                .orElseThrow(() -> problem(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT, "Unknown employee", "No employee " + employeeId + "."));
        return RequestView.of(requests.save(new LeaveRequest(employee, start, end, days, reason)));
    }

    /**
     * One transaction: the request and the employee are loaded into one persistence context, changed in memory, and
     * written together when the method returns. There is no save() call, and none is needed.
     */
    @Transactional
    ApprovalView approve(long id) {
        LeaveRequest request = pending(id);
        Employee employee = request.getEmployee();
        if (employee.getBalanceDays() < request.getDays()) {
            throw problem(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT, "Not enough leave",
                    employee.getName() + " has " + employee.getBalanceDays() + " days left; this request needs " + request.getDays() + ".");
        }
        request.approve();
        return new ApprovalView(id, request.getStatus().name(), request.getDays(), employee.getId(), employee.getBalanceDays());
    }

    RequestView reject(long id) {
        LeaveRequest request = pending(id);
        request.reject();
        return RequestView.of(request);
    }

    ApprovalView cancel(long id) {

        if (request.getStatus() != LeaveRequest.Status.APPROVED) {
            throw problem(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "Not approved", "Leave request " + id + " is " + request.getStatus() + "; only approved leave can be cancelled.");

    }

        return requests.findWithEmployeeById(id)
                .orElseThrow(() -> problem(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Leave request not found", "No leave request " + id + "."));

        LeaveRequest request = find(id);

A Foundations station: the considerations to know, no runbook.

Where transactions belong
On the service method that owns one business change. Not on repositories one by one, and not around HTTP work.
Self-invocation
@Transactional works through a Spring proxy: a call from inside the same class skips it. A classic way to get exactly this station's bug.
open-in-view
Off here. On (Spring's default), it keeps entities loadable during the response, which hides where the transaction really ends.
Retries
A 409 Changed meanwhile is safe to retry after reloading; approval checks PENDING again, so a retry never deducts twice.
Audit
HR needs who approved what and when; this station keeps only the status. A real system records the decision as its own row.

Interview takeaways

What is the persistence context?

The set of entities Hibernate tracks in one session, usually one transaction. It returns the same object for the same row, and at flush writes every change it finds by dirty checking.

Why did save() not save the balance?

The request was detached, so save() merged it: Hibernate copied its columns onto a managed copy. The employee association is not cascaded, so the employee's changes were not copied, and the employee itself was never managed.

Is there an update() in Spring Data JPA?

No. save() on a managed entity does nothing; on a new one it persists; on a detached one it merges and returns a different, managed object. Keep using the returned one.

What can @DataJpaTest hide?

Each test runs in a transaction, so code that forgets its own transaction still works in the test. Test the real entry point without a test transaction as well.

How do you stop two approvals deducting twice?

Check the status inside the transaction and add @Version: the second commit finds a changed version and fails, which you answer with 409. A pessimistic lock is the alternative.
